articles.title: How I convinced Chris Wallace to interview Dolly Parton
articles.summary: “Should I interview Dolly Parton?” I looked up from my desk to find Chris Wallace standing in my office. This was not a particularly unusual occurrence, since Wallace’s office was next to mine, and we would sometimes pop in on each other to compare notes. I was the managing editor of Fox News’s D.C. bureau…
articles.body:
I looked up from my desk to find Chris Wallace standing in my office.

This was not a particularly unusual occurrence, since Wallace’s office was next to mine, and we would sometimes pop in on each other to compare notes. I was the managing editor of Fox News’s D.C. bureau at the time, while Wallace hosted “Fox News Sunday.”

“Yes,” I replied without knowing further context. “You should absolutely interview her. She is nothing less than a national treasure.”

Wallace expressed surprise at my enthusiasm, saying I didn’t strike him as a country music aficionado.

“I’m not,” I replied. “It’s not about the genre. It’s about her songwriting.”

Wallace was known for hard-hitting interviews on policy and politics, so I worried that he might consider Dolly Parton a bit out of his lane. I decided to put on the full-court press.

“You have to interview her,” I blurted. “I honestly believe she’s one of the greatest songwriters America has ever produced.”

I stipulated that I was not an expert on songwriting or country music or even Dolly Parton. But of the dozen or so country songs I’ve ever downloaded (amid thousands of songs in other genres), all of them are by Dolly Parton.

“Not just made famous by Parton,” I emphasized to Wallace. “Actually written by her. I mean, you just cannot ignore the enormity of her songwriting.”

For starters, it is well known that Parton wrote two of her most monumental songs — “Jolene” and “I Will Always Love You” — in one epic creative burst. (It was long believed she wrote them on the same day, but Parton later clarified the process may have stretched into several days.)

The results of that one burst would have been enough to assure the legacy of any mortal songwriter. But Parton wrote so many more masterpieces during an astonishing career that spanned seven decades.

Poignant songs of sadness, like “Coat of Many Colors” and “To Daddy.” Dark songs of betrayal, like “Little Sparrow” and “Dagger Through the Heart.” Wistful songs of lost love, like “The Grass is Blue” and “Do I Ever Cross Your Mind?”

So much melancholy for an otherwise upbeat icon who seemed to radiate good vibes at all times. Fittingly, amid all those sorrowful songs, there was a thread of hopefulness that became her trademark. Take, for example, the opening lines to yet another Parton classic, “Light of a Clear Blue Morning”:

But everything’s gonna work out just fine

Of course, Wallace didn’t need much convincing. He jumped at the chance to interview Dolly Parton. And given my admiration for her, he invited me to the interview.

As the big day approached, I mentally prepared to thank Parton for the various specific songs that meant so much to me. But when she walked through that door in February 2018, I chickened out and resorted to a vague statement about how I was a big fan.

Parton proved just as sweet and down-to-earth as you’d expect. She chatted good-naturedly and posed for a photo. She had me sit down while she remained standing because I’m so tall (6 feet, 7 inches) and she was so short (5 feet). Honestly, she couldn’t have been nicer.

The interview took place at the Library of Congress because Parton was about to present the library with her newest children’s book, “Coat of Many Colors.”

Based on the song of the same name, the book tells the story of Parton’s mother sewing rags into a coat for Dolly, one of 12 children in a family that eked out a hardscrabble existence in the Great Smoky Mountains of east Tennessee.

Of course, Parton would go on to enormous success. Her signature charity, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, has given hundreds of millions of books to schoolchildren. Parton herself literally went from rags to riches.

At the end of her interview with Wallace, Parton burst into song, a cappella, reminding us, yet again, of why she will be remembered as one of America’s greatest songwriters:

And my coat of many colors that my mama made for me

Made only from rags, but I wore it so proudly

And although we had no money, I was rich as I could be

In my coat of many colors my mama made for me

articles.title: Blue states launch new suit to stop Trump’s mail-in voting restrictions
articles.summary: Democratic-controlled states brought a new lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s mail-in voting restrictions on Wednesday, hoping they’ll find better success after the Supreme Court ruled they sued prematurely. The high court found the states had no right to sue over the president’s executive order that he signed in the spring. But it left open the possibility that someone…
articles.body:
Democratic-controlled states brought a new lawsuit challenging the Trump administration’s mail-in voting restrictions on Wednesday, hoping they’ll find better success after the Supreme Court ruled they sued prematurely.

The high court found the states had no right to sue over the president’s executive order that he signed in the spring. But it left open the possibility that someone could still try to sue over the U.S. Postal Service’s plan to implement it.

The Postal Service formally published its final rule on Wednesday. The states argue it means their case is now ripe.

“Congress has not afforded USPS any authority whatsoever to set rules for federal elections or mail voting, even though Americans have cast ballots by mail for generations,” the lawsuit states, using an abbreviation for the U.S. Postal Service.

The case is co-led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington. It heads to U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, an appointee of former President Obama who has been overseeing the legal fight for months.

The Hill has reached out to a Department of Justice (DOJ) spokesperson for comment.

The Postal Service’s final rule mandates that states’ mail-in ballots meet design requirements — such as unique barcodes and an official logo — and that the states upload lists of voters who are eligible to vote by mail. If a ballot doesn’t meet the specifications or someone isn’t on the submitted list, the Postal Service will refuse to deliver it. It’s part of President Trump’s broader, years-long campaign targeting mail voting.

The president’s critics have condemned his order as overreaching into states’ authority to manage their own elections.

The states’ new lawsuit landed just as the judge cleared the way for USPS. Talwani on Wednesday agreed the Supreme Court’s recent directive compels her to wipe all her previous injunctions.

Even so, she cautioned that the plaintiffs could now have a case that USPS has finalized its rule.

The clock is ticking, with some states set to start sending out mail ballots in a matter of days.

articles.title: Appeals court declines to toss McIver case as panel splits on selective prosecution claims
articles.summary: A federal appeals court declined to toss the case against Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.), even as the panel split over a matter in which she is accused of attacking law enforcement with her forearms in a scuffle with immigration officials. The ruling on Wednesday from the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals comes as McIver has pushed to…
articles.body:
A federal appeals court declined to toss the case against Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-N.J.), even as the panel split over a matter in which she is accused of attacking law enforcement with her forearms in a scuffle with immigration officials.

The ruling on Wednesday from the 3rd Circuit Court of Appeals comes as McIver has pushed to get the case dismissed on various grounds, including that her visit to the Delaney Hall detention facility was carried out in her role as a legislative official and should be protected by prosecution under the Speech or Debate Clause.

The three-judge panel declined to toss the case on a number of grounds raised by McIver, finding that while her inspection of Delaney Hall was protected under the clause, her intervention in the arrest of Newark Mayor Ras Baraka (D) was not.

But one judge dissented, saying McIver’s “plausibly incidental contact” with one of the officers came as she was being impeded from carrying out her legislative duties by touring the controversial detention center.

He also touched on McIver’s claims that the case amounted to a selective prosecution , saying the lawmaker “presented enough [evidence] to obtain discovery on whether this prosecution ‘was intended to prevent [her] exercise of a fundamental right’” to conduct legislative oversight.

The pending arrest against Baraka — who no longer faces charges in the matter — ignited chaos between Democrats there to tour the facility and immigration officials on site.

McIver is accused of having “slammed her forearm into the body” of one immigration officer and “using each of her forearms to forcibly strike” a second.

The appeals court determined those actions were not protected by the clause.

“The Speech or Debate Clause does not provide a blanket protection over ‘all things in any way related to the legislative process,’” Judge Cindy Chung wrote in the majority opinion.

“The nature of the conduct charged in Count One is non legislative. Congresswoman McIver’s physical contact with Victim-1 was not ‘integral’ to the ‘deliberative and communicative processes by which Members participate in committee and House proceedings.’”

The ruling determined charges related to those two incidents should stand but remanded the case back to the district court to review a third count that broadly incorporated all “efforts to hinder, impede the arrest of the Mayor.”

A second opinion from Judge Thomas Ambro dissented in part, saying his colleagues were too quick to determine that some of her actions could not be considered tied to her legislative role, saying the second count faced by McIver was at least “ambiguously” legislative.

“When an Executive Branch official prevents a Member from entering a DHS [Department of Homeland Security] facility, she is denied effective access to an oversight inspection, the investigative tool federal law supplies Members in this context,” Ambro wrote, adding that “her access to the facility depended on circumventing him somehow.”

Ambro also said the court should at least grant McIver further discovery on whether she is being selectively prosecuted.

He wrote that among lawmakers’ protections are “freedom from fear that the Executive will use criminal prosecution to punish legislators for their oversight and political opposition.”

“My colleagues believe vindication of this right is beyond our jurisdiction. I disagree. And where, as here, a legislator has presented evidence that her prosecution was brought as an act of political retaliation, I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter—not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote, saying she deserved to know “whether [the case] punishes her for doing her job as a Member of Congress with specific oversight responsibilities.”

articles.title: Maverick Democrat surges with Republicans as his own party turns on him, stoking talk of GOP switch
articles.summary: John Fetterman now holds a 73% favorability among Pennsylvania Republicans, surpassing Dave McCormick's 63%, as party switch speculation grows.
articles.body: Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, a centrist Democrat known for bashing his party's left flank, is more popular among Keystone State Republicans than their own GOP senator, Sen. Dave McCormick, according to a new poll. The release of the poll this week by the New York Times, Philadelphia Inquirer and Siena University is further evidence that Fetterman, who at times breaks with his party and aligns with President Donald Trump, and who is a frequent guest on the Fox News Channel, has become increasingly popular among Republicans. The survey may boost speculation that the first-term senator could potentially bolt the Democrats and become a Republican. But Fetterman has denied that he plans to leave the Democratic Party. Nearly 3 in 4 Republican registered voters in Pennsylvania (73%) held a favorable opinion of Fetterman, according to the poll. That's 10 points higher than the 63% of Republicans in the state who viewed McCormick favorably. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB The 73% of Republicans who view Fetterman favorably is a major increase from the 25% who said the same thing in 2024, two years after the senator was elected. But Fetterman's standing among Democrats continued to sink, according to the poll. Just 22% of registered Democrats in Pennsylvania said they had a favorable view of Fetterman, while 63% viewed him unfavorably. That's a dramatic reversal from two years ago, when 74% of Democrats viewed Fetterman favorably. The survey also indicated that by a 49%-35% margin independents held a favorable view of Fetterman. Matt Beynon, a veteran Pennsylvania-based Republican consultant, told Fox News Digital, "I think a lot of Republicans appreciate the fact that Senator Fetterman is willing to stick his thumb in the radical wing of his party’s eye on issues like antisemitism." WHAT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM RACES SHOW Fetterman's growing popularity among Republicans has fueled speculation that he leave the Democratic Party before potentially facing a primary challenge when he's up for re-election in 2028. The senator, who is a strong supporter of Israel, has increasingly railed against fellow Democrats who have criticized Israeli leaders over their ongoing war against Hamas in Gaza. Fetterman has said he has "no plans" to leave the Democratic Party. But he added if Democrats officially became the "anti-Israel party," count him out. "My long-term concern has been with the Democratic Party, as I am a member of that, is that our party is going to back away and turn their back to Israel," he said last month at a Hill Nation Summit in Washington, D.C. "If our party ever becomes, and just makes it official, the anti-Israel party, that’s when I would leave because that’s been a moral clarity for me." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) and other Senate Republicans have reached out to Fetterman regarding a party switch. "I have had conversations with him in the past, as have many of my colleagues about the challenges he faces in his caucus. And there are many of us who, I think, would welcome the opportunity to have him join the Republican conference, but ultimately that’s a decision that’s up to him," Thune told reporters in July. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But Beynon said that regardless of Fetterman's growing popularity among Republicans, "when it comes time for the Senator’s re-election campaign in 2028, those same voters will be reminded that John Fetterman votes with Democrats more than 90% of the time." Fox News Digital reached out to the senator's office for comment regarding the new poll, but did not receive a response at the time this story was published.

articles.title: Charlamagne knocks Jeffries over Kushner meeting: ‘Yo Hakeem, we don’t believe you’
articles.summary: Charlamagne Tha God slammed House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) over his private meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, accusing the Democratic leader of undermining his own attacks on Trump and his allies. “Yo Hakeem, we don’t believe you,” Charlamagne said Tuesday on “The Breakfast Club,” days after The New York Times reported Sunday…
articles.body:
Charlamagne Tha God slammed House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) over his private meeting with Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law, accusing the Democratic leader of undermining his own attacks on Trump and his allies.

“Yo Hakeem, we don’t believe you,” Charlamagne said Tuesday on “The Breakfast Club,” days after The New York Times reported Sunday that Jeffries and Kushner met privately ahead of November’s midterms.

Jeffries had sought to quell backlash over the meeting by saying “no one from the Trump Cartel is getting a pass.” The House Democratic leader has said Kushner, an informal Trump administration adviser, initiated the meeting. The two reportedly met to discuss common ground issues such as housing and affordability.

Charlamagne argued Democrats shouldn’t use dire language to describe Trump and his movement while privately seeking common ground with people in the president’s orbit.

“Saying people are threats to democracy and fascists and crooks — when you say that, and then we have private meetings with them, working with them, it undermines all of that,” he said.

Kushner, who is married to Trump’s eldest daughter, Ivanka Trump, does not hold an official position in the administration, but he has worked as a foreign envoy in major conflicts, including in Iran.

News of the meeting sparked criticism from some Democrats, prompting Jeffries to defend his decision. In a video posted Monday, Jeffries said he was willing to discuss ways to bring down costs for Americans but insisted that would not stop Democrats from scrutinizing the Trump administration.

“We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law and be guided by the Constitution beginning on day one. And hold the crooks accountable.”

“That’s why Hakeem is getting this smoke, that’s why he’s getting this backlash from people,” he said.

He also questioned why Democratic leaders appear more willing to find common ground with Trump allies than with colleagues in their own party, including progressives.

“I also don’t understand why Democrats have more smoke with people in their own party, like the DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] or anyone labeled a socialist, than they do with MAGA,” Charlamagne said.

articles.title: Philadelphia DA says he'll keep piece of Trump's White House ballroom 'after we all blow it up'
articles.summary: Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said Tuesday he expects President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom to one day be blown up in an “official ceremony."
articles.body: Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner said Tuesday he was going to keep a piece of President Donald Trump's White House ballroom as a paperweight "after we all blow it up." "In about 10 to 15 years, we are all going to be sitting here with smiles on our faces," Krasner said, according to video footage obtained by WCAU. "And I'm going to have a paperweight sitting on my desk. And do you know what that paper weight's going to be? It's going to be a piece of the ballroom after we blow it up." Krasner, who has previously called Trump a fascist and said he would hunt down Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, made the comments while speaking at George Washington's historic home in Philadelphia during the city's annual slavery commiseration, according to WCAU. DEM JUSTICES SLAP SOROS-BACKED PHILLY DA WITH POWER STRIP IN STUNNING DECISION: 'NOT RELIABLE' Krasner first called Trump "a pain in the a–," to which an audience member responded, "No, he's the devil!" Krasner then responded, "He's the devil, alright, well there is some evidence to that effect." "The man himself is the embodiment of hate. He is the embodiment of ignorance. He is the embodiment of depriving people of their vote and their education. That's who he is," Krasner continued. TRUMP ORDERS SIGNS OUTSIDE SMITHSONIAN MUSEUM AMID ROW OVER ITS DEPICTION OF AMERICAN HISTORY Krasner was specifically bashing Trump for deciding to replace a slavery exhibit at the Washington home under a March executive order titled, "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History." Under the order, the National Park Service replaced the panels dedicated to showcasing the history of George Washington's slaves with more broad displays of U.S. history. A protracted legal battle between the city and the Trump administration most recently saw a federal appeals court side with the federal government and rule that Philadelphia had no legal right to dictate the content of the displays at the federally owned site. JUDGE BLOCKS PHILADELPHIA LAW TARGETING MASKED FEDERAL OFFICERS Despite the city's loss to the federal government in the legal fight, Krasner remained defiant. "This memorial will be here, the educational content will be here," Krasner railed Tuesday. "People will be coming to see it, not for a year or two, or not even 20 years. They will be coming to see it as long as this federal park is here." EXCLUSIVE: KENNEDY CENTER BOARD MOVES TO NAME GROUNDS ‘PRESIDENT DONALD J TRUMP PLAZA' "But let me tell you what will not be here," he continued. "There will not be a ballroom. There will not be a Kennedy Center renamed for a fool," Krasner said. Krasner did specify that the envisioned demolition would be "in an official ceremony, just to be clear, in an official ceremony we're gonna blow it up and we're gonna give the taxpayers their money back by selling old pieces as paperweights, and I'm gonna have one on my desk." WHITE HOUSE SEIZES ON DELAYED OBAMA PRESIDENTIAL CENTER OPENING TO CROWN TRUMP ‘BUILDER-IN-CHIEF’ The White House fired back at Krasner's comments about the ballroom project. "President Trump continues to implement long-overdue and necessary renovations to beautify the People’s House as we approach our great Nation’s 250th anniversary of independence. Thanks to the Builder-in-Chief, the White House will be properly glorified and remain in excellent condition for generations to come. Only people who suffer from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome would find a problem with that," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to Fox News Digital. Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence." Fox News Digital contacted Philadelphia's Justice Department for further comment.

articles.title: Federal judge lifts nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions
articles.summary: A federal judge in Boston on Wednesday lifted a nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions, temporarily clearing the way for the Trump administration to begin implementing them ahead of the November midterms. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani granted the Justice Department’s request to reconsider her earlier injunction in the wake of a Supreme Court ruling…
articles.body:
A federal judge in Boston on Wednesday lifted a nationwide block on mail-in voting restrictions, temporarily clearing the way for the Trump administration to begin implementing them ahead of the November midterms.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani granted the Justice Department’s request to reconsider her earlier injunction in the wake of a Supreme Court ruling that found a separate lawsuit challenging President Trump’s order was premature.

“In sum, the court finds that, in light of the Supreme Court’s decision in Trump v. California, Plaintiff Organizations are not likely to prevail as to ripeness without amending their complaint to reflect the fact that a Final Rule has now issued,” Talwani wrote in a nine-page order .

The case was brought by the League of Women Voters and other voting rights groups, who are expected to file a supplemental complaint now that the Postal Service has finalized its rule.

articles.title: Meta settles for $17B in landmark social media case
articles.summary: Plus: 🎤Looking back on Dolly Parton’s legacy {beacon} It’s Wednesday. How many Dolly Parton videos did you watch yesterday? Send us some of your favorites and we’ll share throughout the week. We’ll get it started with this classic duet with Kenny Rogers. In today’s issue: Meta pays $17B to settle…
articles.body:
It’s Wednesday. How many Dolly Parton videos did you watch yesterday? Send us some of your favorites and we’ll share throughout the week.

We’ll get it started with this classic duet with Kenny Rogers.

Programming note : We’re Joshua Feldstein and Abigail Walker , filling in for Cate today. Please send us your tips, comments and story ideas to jfeldstein@thehill.com and awalker@thehill.com.

Manuel Balce Ceneta, Associated Press file

Meta reached a settlement worth up to $17 billion in a case brough by state attorneys general accusing the company of intentionally making its platforms addictive to children.

“Meta has agreed to make massive transformations that will reduce the risk of harm from its platforms — and will do it within months,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said in a statement Wednesday. The settlement still needs to be approved by a judge.

According to a report by The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro , California and 28 other states filed the lawsuit against Meta back in 2023, accusing the parent company of Facebook and Instagram of implementing features that make teens and younger children hooked to the apps.

Playing by the rules : Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mohoney said that the settlement includes a “new set of rules governing teens’ use of social media.”

Mahoney encouraged companies like TikTok and YouTube to follow suit when it comes to implementing child safety frameworks into their platforms.

Facebook and Instagram could see time limit restrictions for those younger than 18 and changes to the platforms’ notifications, according to Bonta.

FIGHT GOES ON : On Tuesday, Snap, the parent company of Snapchat, became the latest company accused of failing to protect children.

Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday (R) filed a lawsuit alleging that Snapchat knowingly lied about the frequency of harmful content that appeared on the app, and that features like 24-hour posts and Snap Streaks can make children addicted.

“Once they have you signed up and logged in, you are officially in their clutches,” Sunday said at a press conference on Tuesday. “From there, Snapchat essentially says good luck getting out.”

According to Nazzaro , the lawsuit comes just weeks after the attorney general announced a complaint against TikTok for similar allegations.

President Trump bounced back from a rough week with two wins last night in key GOP primary races .

Sen. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) won the Republican primary to fill the South Carolina Senate seat vacated by her brother, the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R.-S.C.).

Graham, who was endorsed by Trump, beat out Rep. Ralph Norman (R-S.C.) by almost 5 percentage points. Her win arrives despite a high-profile debate flub that some saw as disqualifying .

In her Tuesday night victory speech, Graham praised the president, telling supporters that “South Carolina is truly Trump country.”

Norman was, predictably, less appreciative of the president’s role in the race.

“The president got involved. He has that right; that’s his prerogative,” Norman said during his concession speech last night, adding he “never understood” Trump’s decision. The comment drew audible booing from his crowd.

Trump-backed former state Sen. Mike Mazzei (R-Okla.) won the Oklahoma gubernatorial primary against the state’s attorney general, Gentner Drummond .

The victory was slim . Drummond trailed Mazzei by just half a point, according to Decision Desk HQ.

Drummond drew Trump’s ire with his opposition to a $4M aluminum smelter pushed by the president. He also criticized Trump’s decision to drop a tariff on imported beef and hike up tariffs on Canadian goods.

“I’m unafraid to disagree with the president when he’s wrong, and he’s wrong on tariffs. He’s wrong on importing cheap beef,” Drummond said in a Sunday interview with NewsNation.

While applauding Mazzei, Trump lashed out at Drummond, writing on Truth Social, “Meanwhile, his Runoff Election Opponent, Gentner Drummond, is a FAKE Republican.”

Democratic socialist N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas won the Democratic primary for Oklahoma Senate.

Thomas crushed opponent Jim Priest (D) in the initial June primary by nearly 20 points and expanded that margin in the runoff. The win represents another victory for the party’s left-wing faction and suggests that its policies appeal to Democratic voters even in deep red corners of the country. She will now face Rep. Kevin Hern (R) in November.

“They’re wanting a different vision, and I have a different vision as a progressive myself,” Thomas told an Oklahoma outlet last month. “Most countries that have socialism, they are thriving.”

Yesterday felt like a national celebration of Dolly Parton’s life as the world mourned her death at the age of 80.

The country music superstar/philanthropist/actress/fashion icon died following a “brief battle” with cancer , Parton’s representative Marcel Pariseau told The Hill.

Former Presidents Clinton, Obama, Bush and Biden alongside President Trump all paid tribute to the late country singer, while Trump also ordered flags across the country to fly at half-staff for a week.

“There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

We will always love you : Parton’s notable hit songs included “Jolene,” “9 to 5,” “Here You Come Again” and “I Will Always Love You,” which turned into a mega hit with Whitney Houston’s version.

Parton used her writing royalties from Houston’s version to pay for band equipment at majority Black schools across America. She also founded “Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library,” a non-profit that provided free books to thousands of children around the world.

She helped mentor many up-and-coming country singers including Miley Cyrus and Carrie Underwood.

Immigrant visa appointments have been placed on hold by the Trump administration, just a week after a federal judge vacated Trump’s policy that would have suspended visa processing from 75 countries.

Why? A State Department spokesperson told The Hill on Wednesday that the pause comes after the decision to carry out an “in-depth training” for consular officers to screen applicants, according to The Hill’s Laura Kelly .

“A more prosperous American means ensuring that visa applicants are not likely to become a public charge, as defined under U.S. law and regulation, and not likely to become dependent on U.S. public benefits reserved for qualified Americans in need,” the State Department said Wednesday.

Legal pushback : U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas rejected the Trump administration’s policy on Friday that suspended visa processing from 75 countries including Iran, Russia and Afghanistan.

Vargas, who was appointed by former President Biden, argued that a person’s nationality does not mean they may not be able to support themselves in the U.S.

Vargas argued that Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority with the policy.

Did Howard Lutnick blow up the Canada talks?

Recent reporting from the New York Times and Bloomberg found that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was a major factor in the collapse of discussions between the nations. According to the reports, Lutnick was particularly critical of reducing auto and aluminum tariffs on Canada.

The Hill’s Mallory Willson wrote that Lutnick “said instead that only a certain volume of aluminum should get lower tariff rates, and that heavy trucks should not have tariffs lowered like cars.”

The Blame Game : While Canadians are putting at least some of the blame on Lutnick, the U.S.’s metal industry was privately pleased with his intervention.

On Tuesday, Canada announced the implementation of tariffs on around 700 U.S. products. The new levies, retaliation for fresh U.S. tariffs, are scheduled to kick in Sept. 8

The WNBA’s Chicago Sky has banned former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom from the team’s matches after he got into a verbal altercation with Chicago’s Natasha Cloud . Kanter was ejected from the game following the incident.

Iran and Oman said Tuesday that they are setting up the framework for a temporary passage for commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. Omani Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi said the country is having “constructive” progress with Iran.

The U.S. military launched a strike on an alleged drug boat in the Caribbean Tuesday night, killing four people on board. Commander Gen. Francis L. Donovan said he ordered the strike due to the vessel’s signs of “narco-trafficking.”

articles.title: Blanche rips Philadelphia district attorney over promise to blow up White House ballroom

And it’s disgusting that a district attorney in Philadelphia, who, by…
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche on Wednesday ripped into the Philadelphia district attorney for suggesting that the White House ballroom would be blown to bits while noting that he was entitled to a piece of the shrapnel as a keepsake.

“The ballroom is being built. And it’s disgusting that a district attorney in Philadelphia, who, by the way, is a city with its own problems, is so focused on what the president is doing in the White House,” Blanche said during a Wednesday appearance on Fox News’s “America’s Newsroom.”

The attorney general’s remarks were made in response to Philadelphia District Attorney Larry Krasner, who is a Democrat.

“In about 10 to 15 years, we are all going to be sitting here with smiles on our faces. And I’m going to have a paperweight sitting on my desk,” Krasner said during a Tuesday press conference .

“And do you know what that paperweight’s going to be? It’s going to be a piece of the ballroom after we blow it up,” he added.

His comments echo those of his party members who have critiqued the ballroom as an illegal project that will cost taxpayers millions of dollars.

In total, the project is projected to cost $600 million and will be funded by a combination of taxpayer dollars and private donations.

President Trump has referred to the ballroom as a “gift” to the American people that will be equipped with state-of-the-art security features to protect future leaders and their guests from drone strikes and attacks.

“The people that are opposing the ballroom are people that, in my opinion, are very disloyal to our country,” Trump said in the Oval Office last week .

“And I think we’re doing well. I think we’re way ahead of schedule. We’re under budget. It’s going to be the most beautiful ballroom of its kind,” he said.

Meanwhile, Blanche has defended the legality of the project, arguing that existing statutes surrounding presidential authority allow for the ballroom’s construction.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation has objected to that stance in court in a case that is now being reviewed by the Supreme Court.

Trump has received approval to move forward with the ballroom’s construction while justices further consider the project’s legality.

articles.body:
Maine Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson is blasting Vice President Vance for going after members of his party over their response to a federal immigration officer fatally shooting a man in Maine earlier this summer.

“JD Vance is a dirtbag. There’s a young man that had a Social Security number, he had a job. I mean, he had a life, he had a family,” Jackson said in a video he posted to social media .

During a rally Monday in Brewer, Maine , Vance noted the Trump administration is still investigating Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer David Brouillette fatally shooting 25-year-old Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a native of Colombia living in the U.S.

But the vice president said Democratic lawmakers voicing concerns about the shooting, which occurred on July 13, appear “far more worried about a shooting involving an illegal alien than they are about the fact that tens of thousands of Mainers died from fentanyl overdoses by that poison brought into our community.”

Vance added, “And so my message to the Democrats who are so worried about that situation is to say: Have a little bit of perspective.

“We can absolutely investigate every shooting, and we will, but we can also secure our border and ensure that that poison stops coming into our country. And that is our priority, and that’s our emphasis.”

Jackson, though, remarked that the vice president ought to “have some damn perspective of his own.”

The Senate hopeful continued, “I mean, you don’t even know what the hell’s going on,” referring to Vance.

“You got a rogue agency that’s going around, pulling people out of their homes,” he said, referencing ICE. Jackson later said Vance did not “give a s‑‑‑” about Durán Guerrero.

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

Jackson’s opponent , GOP Sen. Susan Collins, joined fellow Maine Sen. Angus King (I) in calling for an independent probe into the shooting last month.

But in his video, Jackson questioned whether Collins agreed with Vance’s position on the shooting.

“I’ll you what, concerns and all that does nothing for all of us, does nothing for that family and I’m sick of your concerns,” Jackson said of Collins.

Officials from the Homeland Security Department have argued the ICE officer shot Durán Guerrero, who was not the target of the operation and was allegedly attempting to leave the premises in his car, out of fear for public safety .

articles.title: Judge allows Trump’s mail-in ballots plan to proceed, at least for now
articles.summary: A federal judge allowed President Donald Trump to move forward with his mail-in ballots plan after the Supreme Court ruling on Monday.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — A federal judge on Wednesday allowed President Donald Trump, at least temporarily, to move forward with his effort to exert federal control over mail-in ballots ahead of the midterm elections. The decision by Boston-based U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani to lift an injunction that applied nationwide follows a Supreme Court decision favoring Trump in a similar case on Monday. But with litigation moving swiftly, there remains a strong chance that key aspects of Trump’s mail-in ballots executive order will be blocked at some stage, possibly as soon as later on Wednesday. The executive order directs the U.S. Postal Service to, among other things, track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters. Multiple legal challenges to the proposal, which conflicts with the states’ traditional role in administering elections, are pending. Trump has frequently criticized mail-in ballots even though they are widely used by Republicans and Democrats all across the country. The Supreme Court on Monday lifted a nationwide injunction that had blocked the executive order in a case brought by California and 22 other states. That ruling left in place a second injunction in a separate case brought by various groups including the League of Women Voters, which Talwani lifted on Wednesday. She is overseeing both cases. The Supreme Court, divided 6-3, concluded that Talwani had acted too hastily in ruling on the executive order, but did not weigh in on whether the underlying proposal or the Postal Service regulation to implement it is lawful. The Trump administration argued that the injunction in the League of Women Voters case should be lifted in light of the Supreme Court ruling, as the same logic applies in both cases. Talwani reluctantly agreed, while making it clear that the challengers have “substantial arguments that might persuade the Supreme Court to reach a different result” if the litigation ultimately returns to the justices. Lawyers in the cases brought by the League of Women’s Voters and the states are both set to challenge the regulation. Talwani, appointed by President Barack Obama, in a separate order issued on Tuesday said that the Trump administration violated her original injunction because it had moved forward with issuing the Postal Service regulation despite her instruction not to do so. But she elected not to impose any sanctions on the government, saying only that she was “identifying the violation.”

articles.title: Poll: Data centers gain massive support — they don’t waste water!
articles.summary: Data centers create jobs and prosperity, and the amount of water they use is a drop in the bucket.
articles.body:
Arguments about data centers are reaching a fever pitch, with so many Americans saying they don’t want these things in their town. Just look at how angry people are getting.

But one major point of contention is based on an apparent lie: that data centers consume a huge amount of water. It turns out that this is simply not the case at all, and in fact, the water they do use — which is much less than is used, for example, for farming — is easily recycled. And importantly, when people learn this fact, their views on data centers changed rapidly .

After people are told that data centers can reuse the water, they become 31 points more supportive of building them. That suggests to me that when people say they’re against data centers, they’re not saying they’re against AI or technology or anything of that nature.

What they’re concerned about is resource depletion, and they have been told — in some cases by hostile foreign actors — that data centers are going to strain the power grid and use up all the water and pollute the rivers and make a lot of noise. None of those things are true, and the people trying to convince you they are true are far-left degrowth activists who don’t want us to build anything, and would in fact like to see communist China outcompete the U.S.

Now, there is some genuine conservative opposition to the centers as well. The Federalist’s John Daniel Davidson, for instance, wrote on X : “Bringing in data centers to save a dying town is like bringing in casinos and race tracks to save a dying city.”

That’s an absurd comparison, of course. Casinos and race tracks make my money via the promotion of vice — which, by the way, I’m perfectly fine with — whereas data centers are building the infrastructure that makes modern life possible, and harming absolutely no one in the process. In fact, their existence even allows local governments to lower your property taxes, which sounds like a pretty good deal to me.

But also, if not data centers, then what is your plan to revitalize dying American towns? I keep hearing from national conservatives that they want to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. and build things here, but if we can’t even build a data center because it’s too noisy, how are we possibly going to have a domestic industrial policy? We’re just going to end up doing nothing, and stagnating because of it. Which is exactly what our enemies want. It’s what the left seems to want. It should not be what conservatives want.

To be clear, there’s a significant contingent of MAGA that sees through this. According to Echelon Insights , Republicans that are “more conservative, male, and MAGA” are the most supportive of data centers within the Republican coalition. That’s not so surprising — President Trump himself remains entirely supportive of building more data centers.

When he’s right, he’s right. Data centers create jobs and prosperity, and the amount of water they use is a drop in the bucket. Tell your friends and neighbors — spread the word!

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

articles.title: Federal judge blocks Texas drag show ban, citing Dolly Parton
articles.summary: A federal judge on Tuesday struck down, for the second time, a Texas law that would have restricted public drag performances in the state, name-checking the late Dolly Parton in doing so. U.S. District Judge David Hittner ruled that the state Senate Bill 12, which was passed in 2023, violated the First Amendment and “is…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday struck down, for the second time, a Texas law that would have restricted public drag performances in the state, name-checking the late Dolly Parton in doing so.

U.S. District Judge David Hittner ruled that the state Senate Bill 12 , which was passed in 2023, violated the First Amendment and “is an unconstitutional restriction on free speech.”

In the ruling, Hittner wrote that S.B. 12’s definition of banned performances was “unconstitutionally vague.”

“Because the term ‘prurient interest in sex’ is open-ended, S.B. 12 can be used to cherry-pick particular aspects of performances that might be ‘in some sense erotic,'” the judge wrote, according to documents obtained by USA Today.

Hittner referenced country music star Parton, whose death was announced Tuesday, in blocking the ban’s restrictions on shows that appeal to the “prurient interest,” noting people would criticize the “9 to 5” singer “as a voluptuous sex symbol because of her big hair, flamboyant clothes and breast exposure.”

In the ruling , Hittner blocked Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whom the case was filed against, from enforcing the act again.

“Drag has always been a form of free expression, and it is a relief that the court recognized that today,” Brigitte Bandit, a plaintiff in the case, said Tuesday . “As a lifelong Texan, I’m sick of this state trying to censor art and stoke hatred and violence against drag artists and the LGBTQIA+ community.”

The case was originally decided in 2023 by Hittner, who issued an injunction at the time because he said S.B. 12 created “viewpoint discrimination” and was “substantially overbroad as written.”

The 5th Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the injunction and remanded the district court to revisit the challenges made by plaintiffs — 360 Queen Entertainment, Extragrams, The Woodlands Pride, Abilene Pride Alliance and Bandit.

Judge Kurt Engelhardt of the 5th Circuit wrote that the lower court should utilize Supreme Court precedent established in 2024’s Moody v. NetChoice , which narrowed the scope of First Amendment challenges by creating new parameters for evaluation.

S.B. 12 went into effect following that order before Hittner ruled that the Moody test and the appellate court’s ruling “did not disturb” his prior decision, pausing enforcement of the law again.

Paxton slammed Hittner’s ruling on social media Tuesday , calling it a “flawed decision that endangers our children and is an affront to Texas values.”

He confirmed he will be appealing the decision back to the 5th Circuit Court of Appeals, which will consider the case under the Moody test.

articles.title: Hakeem Jeffries dismisses Kushner meeting concerns
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries met privately with Jared Kushner, and everybody has questions.
articles.body:
Hakeem Jeffries met privately with Jared Kushner, and everybody has questions.

The New York Times reported Sunday that the House Democratic leader had a private meeting with President Trump’s son-in-law to discuss potential areas of common ground.

On the surface, that’s politics. Jeffries could soon be Speaker if Democrats win the House, so having conversations with people close to the White House makes sense. Probably would make more sense to people who actually have jobs in the White House, but I digress.

Jeffries then posted this video defending the meeting.

“He asked for a meeting and I took it, to discuss the affordability crisis that exists that is not a hoax. At the same period in time — I shouldn’t have to say it, but I am — no one is going to get a pass. We’re gonna hold every single member of the Trump cartel accountable, beginning on day one,” said the House minority leader.

OK. But I have questions. First, why are you dressed like it’s St. Patrick’s Day?

Jeffries says in that moment he just finished community work, and maybe that’s exactly what happened. But the video felt very intentional and like trying too hard.

Back to Hakeem Jeffries meeting with Jared Kushner. Trump has called Jeffries a “thug” and attacked his intelligence as low IQ, and Jeffries has spent years portraying Trump as extreme and corrupt, vowing to hold him accountable. So meeting with Kushner about affordability doesn’t exactly make sense.

Jeffries has longstanding ties to the pro-Israel political and donor network. Campaign-finance tracking shows roughly $1.7 million in AIPAC-linked support over his political career, depending on how broader affiliated spending is counted. Of course that does not prove AIPAC had anything to do with this meeting, but it is relevant context: Kushner also has longstanding financial and diplomatic connections involving Israel, including large donations to AIPAC.

Take a look at this New York Times headline : “Kushner’s Financial Ties to Israel Deepen Even With Mideast Diplomatic Role”

The Times previously reported that while Kushner was serving in the first Trump administration, his family real estate company received roughly $30 million from one of the largest Israeli insurers. His company also took loans from Bank Hapoalim, Israel’s largest bank.

Again, none of that tells us what was discussed between Kushner and Jeffries, but it tells us this isn’t simply two guys talking about the price of eggs. There are significant political, diplomatic and financial relationships surrounding both men, and that’s why people are asking questions.

Tommy Vietor put it bluntly : “Jared Kushner has no actual government job he just uses his family connections to get money from gulf autocrats and fund corrupt deals. The only way @RepJeffries should work with him is with demands for documents and subpoenas.”

Kushner has no formal government job right now, yet he has extraordinary access to the president and Jeffries could soon have extraordinary power in Congress.

So maybe this meeting really was about affordability. Maybe it was simply a potential Speaker talking to someone who has the president’s ear. But if that’s the case, Democrats deserve more transparency — so why was it a secret?

Jeffries cannot spend years promising to hold the Trump administration accountable and then expect people not to question private meetings with one of Trump’s closest family members.

Lindsey Granger is a NewsNation contributor and co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising.” This column is an edited transcription of her on-air commentary.

articles.title: Former Labor secretary calls Trump’s Canada tariffs ‘irrational’
articles.summary: Former Labor Secretary Robert Reich on Wednesday called President Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on Canadian imports “irrational.” Reich warned in an interview with “Squawk Box” co-host Andrew Ross Sorkin on CNBC that prices would rise, particularly for housing, as a result of the trade war. “And as Canadian wood products become even more expensive, you’re…
articles.body:
Former Labor Secretary Robert Reich on Wednesday called President Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on Canadian imports “irrational.”

Reich warned in an interview with “Squawk Box” co-host Andrew Ross Sorkin on CNBC that prices would rise, particularly for housing, as a result of the trade war.

“And as Canadian wood products become even more expensive, you’re going to see housing becoming, again, even more of a basket case,” Reich, who served under former President Clinton from 1993 to 1997, said. “And in the long term, Treasurys, the effect on mortgage rates –– well, this is a major, important sector of the economy.”

“That is a particular problem for young people trying to get into the housing market,” Reich continued. “I see the Canadian trade war as just irrational, completely and totally irrational.”

The U.S. tariffs on Canada went into effect Saturday and apply to $20 billion in Canadian imports, after negotiations between the two countries failed late Friday. Canada retaliated the next day with tariffs of up to 50 percent on more than 700 American exports, ranging from cheese, metal products made of steel or aluminum, carpets, fish and more.

Reich, responding to Sorkin’s point that voters are widely concerned about affordability and the cost of living, said he would not handle affordability with a trade war, tariffs or a “war in the Middle East,” referring to the Iran war.

“I think all these things are actually making consumers more desperate and everything less affordable,” he continued. “The way you deal with the trade war is you stop it.”

The former Labor secretary called the tariffs “damaging for both sides” and said Trump was “lashing out.”

“You know, if this were a joke, if this were a sort of Mel Brooks movie, that would be one thing,” Reich said, referring to the comedian and filmmaker. “But it’s not a joke. I think our president is simply lashing out because he wants to show dominance. He feels so trapped in Iran. … Canada is just an easy mark for a bully.”

Trump accused Canada of being “among the worst Nations in the World to deal with.”

The president faces a potential clash with Senate Republicans over the trade war’s ramifications for their states, particularly with the November midterm elections not far away.

Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) called the new tariffs imposed on Canada “ a mistake .”

“I really want us to go back to the very friendly, economically beneficial relationship that we have with our Canadian neighbors,” she told News Center Maine. She added that she thought the Trump administration was close to a deal and expressed hope that it “brings an agreement.”

articles.title: Millions of barrels of Iranian oil sit beyond Trump blockade as he vows ‘zero leakage’
articles.summary: Nearly 40 million barrels of Iranian crude sit on tankers near Malaysia, posing a test for Trump's "zero-leakage" sanctions campaign against Tehran.
articles.body: Far from the U.S. warships enforcing a blockade at the mouth of the Persian Gulf, nearly 40 million barrels of Iranian crude are sitting aboard tankers in waters near Malaysia, east of Singapore. The cargo amounts to roughly 20 very large crude carriers’ worth of oil, a floating stockpile that could still give Tehran a way to turn crude already outside the blockade zone into cash even as the blockade sharply restricts fresh exports. The stockpile poses a test for the Trump administration as it moves from military action and a naval blockade toward what the White House calls its financial "endgame" against Tehran. TRUMP’S IRAN CRACKDOWN ‘SUFFOCATING’ REGIME AS OIL WELLS COULD SHUT WITHIN DAYS, BESSENT SAYS Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday launched Operation Economic Outcast, promising a "zero-leakage approach" designed to cut off Iran's remaining sources of revenue after months of pressure on its oil sales, shipping networks and financial enablers. The blockade appears to be making it substantially harder for Iran to export new oil. China’s imports of Iranian crude have fallen to an estimated 534,000 barrels per day so far this month, down from roughly 823,000 barrels per day in July, according to provisional Kpler data reported by Reuters. But millions of barrels that moved beyond the blockade line before it tightened remain within potential reach of buyers. Iran has an estimated 80 million barrels of crude held in floating storage, Reuters reported, with roughly half aboard vessels near Malaysia. That leaves Washington facing a different challenge: stopping Tehran from monetizing oil the blockade did not trap. If Iran can still turn that crude into cash, the regime can use the proceeds to pay for imports and potentially finance efforts to rebuild its military even as the blockade restricts fresh exports. That makes the tankers near Malaysia an early test of whether the administration can deliver the "total isolation" it has promised. CHINA ORDERS FIRMS TO IGNORE US IRAN SANCTIONS, DARING US TO ENFORCE CRACKDOWN "The blockade as it’s currently being practiced and enforced against isn’t really stopping the flow of Iranian oil that’s already past the blockade line," Max Meizlish, a former Treasury official focused on sanctions policy and current senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told Fox News Digital. Iranian oil can move through ship-to-ship transfers, in which cargo is shifted from one tanker to another at sea. The practice can help obscure the oil’s origin before it reaches a buyer, often an independent Chinese refinery. Simply having the crude outside the blockade zone does not automatically give Tehran usable revenue. Iran still needs to deliver the oil, collect payment and move the proceeds through the financial channels it has used to evade sanctions. Treasury has said Iran primarily settles oil sales in Chinese yuan, with exchange houses and front companies helping convert those funds into currencies the regime can use. The department has also previously tied proceeds from Iranian oil sales to the Iranian government, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, weapons development and Tehran’s regional proxies. Meizlish noted that the administration has continued sanctioning Chinese and Hong Kong trading houses, maritime service providers and other entities accused of enabling Iranian sanctions evasion but has stopped short of designating a Chinese financial institution. The U.S. cut the bank off from access to the American financial system in 2012 over dealings with Iran, Meizlish said, but stopped short of placing it on Treasury’s Specially Designated Nationals list. He argued that formally designating the bank could put pressure on its owner, China National Petroleum Corporation, and potentially disrupt a channel used to move Iranian oil revenue. Meizlish noted that the administration has continued sanctioning Chinese and Hong Kong trading houses, maritime service providers and other entities accused of enabling Iranian sanctions evasion, but has so far stopped short of designating a Chinese financial institution. "Secretary Bessent didn’t mention China by name," he said, adding that the issue could become a subject of higher-level engagement between Washington and Beijing. The administration has already targeted the Malaysia route. In April, Treasury sanctioned the Hong Kong-flagged tanker Lynn, saying the vessel conducted a ship-to-ship transfer of Iranian crude off Malaysia before delivering the cargo to China. Meizlish said another option would be to expand pressure on shadow-fleet vessels operating near Malaysia and elsewhere in Asia in an effort to keep that oil from ultimately reaching Chinese buyers. "The U.S. could expand the blockades in that sense by going after shadow fleet tankers, operating, for instance, off the coast of Malaysia, which is a huge hub for illicit ship-to-ship transfers," he said. He said the sharp decline in Chinese purchases suggests the pressure campaign is having an effect, but argued that crude already aboard shadow-fleet tankers remains a potential future source of revenue for Tehran. "There’s a lot more that we can do," Meizlish said. "Unless we expect for this regime to ultimately fall, we should be putting a lot of pressure into interdicting this oil that’s on the market right now on shadow fleet tankers, because this money could eventually go into the regime’s pockets down the road," he said. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER Asked whether the administration planned further action against Iranian oil cargoes and shadow-fleet vessels near Malaysia, a War Department official told Fox News Digital that U.S. forces would continue "global maritime enforcement" to disrupt illicit networks and interdict sanctioned vessels supporting Iran "wherever they operate, at the time and place of our choosing." "Under Operation Economic Outcast, anyone foolish enough to continue doing business with the Iranian regime cannot continue to enjoy access to the global financial system," a Treasury Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "We will cut every remaining economic lifeline Tehran has." Meizlish said money from oil already sitting on shadow-fleet tankers could still wind up in Tehran’s hands and help Iran rebuild military capabilities damaged in the conflict. Going after those tankers would not be simple. The U.S. Navy is already stretched by operations in the Strait of Hormuz and elsewhere, he said, and seizing ships and their cargo can trigger legal fights over ownership, custody and what happens to the oil afterward. He also argued that Washington should look for ways to expand its capacity to pursue shadow-fleet vessels if the Navy cannot do it alone. Bessent’s new campaign goes beyond oil, targeting digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping. He also threatened broader secondary sanctions against entities that continue doing business with Tehran. The drop in Chinese purchases shows Iran is having a harder time getting new oil to market. But millions of barrels are already sitting outside the blockade. Whether Tehran can still sell that oil, and whether Washington is willing to go after it near Malaysia, will help determine how much "zero leakage" actually means.

articles.title: El CEO de Ryanair responde con firmeza a las palabras de Óscar Puente: “Tiene que aprender a restar y sumar”
articles.standfirst: Michael O’Leary aparece tras varios días de cruces de declaraciones entre el ministro de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible y la aerolínea
articles.summary: Michael O’Leary aparece tras varios días de cruces de declaraciones entre el ministro de Transportes y Movilidad Sostenible y la aerolínea
articles.body: Óscar Puente, ministro de Transportes y de Movilidad Sostenible, sigue protagonizando cruces de declaraciones entre Ryanair. El político escribió este mismo miércoles, 27 de agosto, un tuit cargando contra la aerolínea. Cabe recalcar que estas últimas declaraciones recientes llegan apenas dos días después de que el ministro anunciara que la aerolínea irlandesa ha recortado tre millones de asientos en aeropuertos de nuestro país , concretamente, regionales, aumentando la oferta en más de 500.000 plazas en otros centros de España como pueden ser Palma, Madrid o Barcelona. Pues bien, unas horas más tarde, el CEO del grupo Ryanair, Michael O’Leary, respondió de manera tajante al propio Puente con un vídeo en redes sociales de la propia compañía. Michael O’Leary arrancó de la siguiente manera al respecto: “Esta semana he leído afirmaciones falsas del ministro de Transportes, Óscar Puente, diciendo que nuestros recortes en aeropuertos regionales se deben a falta de aviones o de capacidad en Ryanair. Estas afirmaciones son falsas”. El CEO de la aerolínea adjuntó una pizarra con los siguientes datos: “En el verano de 2026, Ryanair operará 648 aviones, 29 más que en el verano de 2025. Con esos aviones adicionales, aumentaremos el tráfico de 208 millones de pasajeros en 2025 a 216 millones en 2026, 8 millones más. “Lamentablemente, nada de ese crecimiento en aviones, rutas o tráfico irá a la España regional, donde el fallido ministro Puente mantiene altas tasas aéreas y costes inasumibles en aeropuertos regionales vacíos. España puede crecer, pero solo con un ministro de Transportes que sepa sumar y restar, y que reconozca que España no es competitiva”, siguió añadiendo al respecto. Asimismo, también recalcó que Puente dice que España tiene de las tasas aéreas de Europa más bajas, algo que según él “no es así”, ya que hasta que nuestro país no las tenga en “cero”, España tendrá las tasas aéreas “altas”. “La única solución es enviarle al ministro Puente esta semana el libro Matemáticas básicas para dummies, porque el ministro Puente es un dummy. Él preside el declive del tráfico en España, mientras que, en el resto de Europa, gracias a los nuevos aviones y rutas de Ryanair, el tráfico no para de crecer. España puede crecer, pero solo cuando Óscar Puente aprenda a sumar, a restar y, quizá, a leer cómo hacer bien las cuentas”, sentenció Michael O’Leary de manera tajante hacia Puente.

articles.title: Democrats condemning Hasan Piker as backlash spreads through party
articles.summary: Hakeem Jeffries called Hasan Piker's remarks about American Jews "dangerous and antisemitic" as top Democrats lined up to condemn the streamer.
articles.body: Prominent Democrats are lining up to condemn far-left streamer Hasan Piker after he warned that American Jews could face violence if they continue to be seen as strongly supporting Israel. The backlash follows a stream last week in which Piker displayed an image of Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, who is Jewish and the Democratic nominee in Michigan's 11th Congressional District. Moss has said a fake audio clip is being circulated that falsely portrays him as saying he ran for Congress solely to ensure continued U.S. support for Israel. "If Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone is going to come around and take action, not against the state of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said. PIKER DEMANDS DEMOCRATS DEFEND HIM FROM ATTACKS, CLAIMS HE’S NO ‘TOXIC RADICAL FORCE' Piker's comments drew criticism from top Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and DNC Chair Ken Martin, as well as lawmakers who have criticized him before. Others who have appeared with Piker or defended engaging with him are now pushing back on his remarks. Here are the Democrats speaking out: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. Jeffries joined the backlash Monday, initially without mentioning Piker by name. The House Democratic leader called the claim that American Jews were inviting violence against themselves "dangerous and antisemitic." Asked on CNN the following day whether he was referring to Piker, Jeffries said yes. "Those comments were dangerous, malicious and antisemitic and should not be tolerated by anyone in the public square," Jeffries said. Rep. Brad Schneider, D-Ill. Schneider was one of the first Democratic lawmakers to publicly take on Piker, calling him an "unapologetic antisemite" in March and warning fellow Democrats against giving a platform to people who espouse hate. PIKER DEMANDS DEMOCRATS DEFEND HIM FROM ATTACKS, CLAIMS HE’S NO ‘TOXIC RADICAL FORCE' Schneider renewed that criticism Tuesday, saying Piker's latest remarks were consistent with his "history of antisemitic statements." "Hasan Piker's hateful ideas and antisemitic remarks have no place in America or our nation's politics," Schneider said. Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich. Slotkin, who had previously criticized Piker and his involvement in Michigan Democratic politics, spoke out again after his latest comments. "No community should face the threat [of] violence for their political views," Slotkin said, rejecting the idea that Jewish Americans should be blamed for antisemitism directed at them. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich. Stevens criticized Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed earlier this year for campaigning with Piker and made clear she would not do the same. Piker was the "exact opposite" of someone she would campaign with, Stevens said. She later said she believed Piker should be condemned. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J. Booker's team had already kept its distance from Piker, turning down an appearance with the streamer over his past comments. Booker went further this week, directly condemning Piker's rhetoric about Jewish Americans and saying it has no place in public discourse. Michigan state Sen. Mallory McMorrow In April, McMorrow criticized Piker's role in Michigan Democratic politics and his inflammatory style. She compared Piker's approach to that of far-right commentator Nick Fuentes, arguing that both use inflammatory rhetoric to attract attention. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J. Gottheimer has been among Piker's most persistent Democratic critics. In April, he joined Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York in introducing a bipartisan House resolution condemning antisemitic rhetoric from Piker and Candace Owens. In an interview on Fox News' "America's Newsroom," Gottheimer praised Jeffries pushback against Piker, calling the streamer’s comments something "right out of the Nazi playbook," emphasizing them as "a call for violence against Jews." Gottheimer on Tuesday also called on House leaders to bring the resolution up for a vote. He also told CNN in an interview that anyone who does not condemn Piker’s comments is "complicit." HASAN PIKER CALLS FOR DEMOCRATS WHO OPPOSE ABDUL EL-SAYED TO BE 'PUNISHED' James Carville Longtime Democratic strategist James Carville drew a line between himself and part of the Democratic Party embracing Piker earlier this month. Carville said he would leave the party if Piker's wing took control, arguing there was no room for both of them under the same political tent. He later told Fox News' "Jesse Watters Primetime" he is not concerned about socialists taking over the Democratic Party, dismissing the party's socialist flank as a "pack of fools" and "a bunch of silly people." Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa. Fetterman earlier this month took aim at El-Sayed over his ties to Piker during Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. "I dare you to continue to campaign with people like Hasan Piker," Fetterman said. Fetterman's comments were aimed primarily at Democrats associating with Piker rather than a direct response to the streamer's latest remarks. Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla. Moskowitz distanced himself from Piker last week after defeating a Democratic primary challenger who had Piker's backing. The Florida Democrat made clear after the race that he wanted no association with Piker or his politics. Rep. Jake Auchincloss, D-Mass. Auchincloss rejected Piker's politics during an appearance on "Fox News Sunday," drawing a clear distinction between the streamer and the Democratic Party. "The Democratic Party does not stand for what Hasan Piker stands for," Auchincloss said. HASAN PIKER STANDS BY 'INTENTIONALLY PROVOCATIVE' CLAIMS THAT HAMAS IS 'A THOUSAND TIMES BETTER' THAN ISRAEL Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich. Scholten issued one of the sharpest responses after Piker's comments about American Jews and Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss. "Hasan Piker's talk of violence against American Jews and directly naming a Michigan elected official and future member of Congress, Jeremy Moss, is unacceptable. Full stop," Scholten said Monday. She also called Piker a "hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe" and said his rhetoric had no place in Michigan or the country. Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss, D Moss, who was directly discussed during Piker's stream, on Monday pushed back after Piker displayed his image while talking about American Jews and Israel. Moss said there was "no room for extremism in Michigan." Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif. Khanna's response was notable because he has appeared on Piker's show and previously defended his decision to engage with the streamer. But on Monday, Khanna rejected Piker's latest argument, saying antisemitism should be condemned unequivocally and that Jewish people and supporters of Israel are not responsible for antisemitism directed at them. Abdul El-Sayed El-Sayed, whose Michigan Senate campaign has faced criticism over his association with Piker, sought to put some distance between his campaign and the streamer after the latest controversy on Monday. El-Sayed said Piker does not speak for him or his campaign and condemned antisemitism. He stopped short, however, of directly condemning Piker himself. DEMOCRATIC MICHIGAN AG ACCUSES HER PARTY OF 'ABSOLUTELY NOT' DOING ENOUGH TO COUNTER ANTISEMITISM DNC Chair Ken Martin Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin joined the criticism Tuesday, bringing the national party's leadership into the dispute. Martin condemned the idea that American Jews should be blamed for hatred, threats or violence directed at them, calling such rhetoric dangerous, wrong and antisemitic. Sen. Jacky Rosen, D-Nev. Rosen, co-chair of the Senate Bipartisan Task Force for Combating Antisemitism, said Piker had used antisemitic tropes before but on Tuesday described his latest remarks as "a new low." The Nevada Democrat rejected the suggestion that Jewish Americans bear responsibility for antisemitism or violence directed at them. Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y. Torres, a longtime Piker critic, again spoke out Tuesday after the streamer's comments about American Jews. The New York Democrat accused Piker of blaming Jewish victims for the antisemitism directed against them, adding to his previous criticism of the streamer. Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Ariz. Stanton joined the Democrats speaking out Tuesday over Piker's latest comments. The Arizona congressman rejected the argument that Jewish Americans bear responsibility for hatred or violence directed against them. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Wednesday will honor the Marines who served during the 2021 Abbey Gate attack in Afghanistan to mark five years since the deadly bombing .

The Aug. 26, 2021, suicide bombing outside Kabul’s airport killed 13 U.S. service members and roughly 170 Afghan civilians as the U.S. carried out its swift withdrawal of troops from Afghanistan under former President Biden.

The ceremony comes as the Trump administration continues its probe of the incident.

The Defense Department earlier this year upgraded the valor awards that were originally given to the service members.

The event is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. EDT.

articles.title: Maryland court blocks Democrats’ redistricting amendment from November ballot
articles.summary: A Maryland court has ruled against a proposed constitutional amendment that could have paved the way for Democrats to redraw the state’s congressional districts ahead of the 2028 elections.
articles.body: A Maryland court has ruled against a proposed constitutional amendment that could have paved the way for Democrats to redraw the state’s congressional districts ahead of the 2028 elections. The ruling Wednesday by a judge in the state’s capital city marks another setback in Democrats’ national attempts to counter a Republican redistricting movement pushed by President Donald Trump ahead of this year’s elections. The judge ruled that the amendment cannot appear on the November ballot, but he paused the effect of that ruling to allow for an appeal to the state Supreme Court. Democrats already control seven of Maryland’s eight congressional seats. Democratic Gov. Wes Moore called lawmakers into a special session in August with a goal of making it easier to claim that final seat. An amendment referred to the ballot by lawmakers seeks to sidestep a court ruling that struck down a previous Democratic redistricting plan in 2022. It would declare that a constitutional requirement for districts to be compact and take into account “natural boundaries” applies only to state legislative districts, not congressional ones. That would allow Democratic state lawmakers to draw congressional districts that cross the Chesapeake Bay, reshaping a district east of the bay that is held by Republican Rep. Andy Harris, chair of the conservative House Freedom Caucus. Anne Arundel County Circuit Court Judge Robert Thompson ruled that lawmakers violated their own deadlines for ballot measures. Earlier this year, lawmakers passed a law signed by Moore that set a July 1 deadline for the secretary of state to certify summaries of all statewide ballot questions to the Maryland State Board of Elections. The state attorney general’s office argued that deadline didn’t apply to the redistricting amendment because lawmakers wrote their own ballot summary for it, using their constitutional authority. The judge disagreed, instead siding with arguments by the conservative Oversight Project and Republican state lawmakers who sued. Thompson also ruled that lawmakers used “intentionally misleading” wording in the ballot question by stating that it merely “clarifies” the Constitution’s redistricting standards. And Thompson said the amendment violates a single-issue requirement in the Constitution by also including a provision that would give the state Supreme Court original jurisdiction in lawsuits over congressional redistricting. “The court has no choice but to enjoin the board of elections from including ballot Question 3 on the general election ballot for November 3, 2026,” Thompson wrote. Earlier this year, the Virginia Supreme Court also invalidated a redistricting ballot measure because of procedural violations by state lawmakers. In that case, voters had already approved an amendment in April authorizing mid-decade redistricting when the court ruled that lawmakers last year had waited too long to take an initial step necessary to qualify it for the ballot. Virginia and Maryland both were seeking to follow the path of California, where voters approved a Democratic-backed amendment authorizing mid-decade redistricting. Democrats hope to gain as many as five congressional seats from California’s redrawn districts, plus an additional seat from new districts in Utah. But Republicans hope to win as many as 16 additional seats from new U.S. House districts enacted in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas. Redistricting typically happens near the beginning of each decade, after new census data is released. But a mid-decade redistricting battle broke out after Trump urged Republican-led states to redraw congressional districts in hopes that it might help Republicans hold onto a slim House majority in this year’s midterm elections.
